An organic light-emitting component may include: a substrate, a first electrode arranged over the substrate, at least one organic functional layer stack configured to emit radiation and arranged over the first electrode, at least one conductive current spreading structure which is arranged on the first electrode and faces the at least one organic functional layer stack, and a second electrode arranged over the at least one organic functional layer stack. The at least one conductive current spreading structure may comprise at least one metal, and may be covered with an inorganic passivation layer. The inorganic passivation layer may comprise a sulfide, a selenide and/or a telluride of the at least one metal. The inorganic passivation layer may be an n-type or p-type semiconductor, such that no current flows between the least one conductive current spreading structure and the at least one organic functional layer stack via the inorganic passivation layer.

The organic light-emitting component comprises a substrate on which a first electrode is arranged. At least one organic functional layer stack is positioned over the first electrode and is configured to emit electromagnetic radiation during operation.

A conductive current-spreading structure is disposed on the first electrode, facing the organic functional layer stack. This structure contains at least one metal and promotes a more uniform distribution of electrical current across the component.

The conductive current-spreading structure may be covered by an inorganic passivation layer comprising a sulfide, selenide, and/or telluride of the metal contained in the current-spreading structure. The passivation layer may be formed as an n-type or p-type semiconductor and configured to prevent current flow between the conductive current-spreading structure and the organic functional layer stack. In this way, the passivation layer electrically isolates the current-spreading structure from the organic layers while allowing the structure to improve current distribution through the first electrode.
outputs.L4:
An organic light-emitting component comprises a substrate, a first electrode, an organic functional layer stack, and a second electrode. To improve the lateral distribution of current across the first electrode, particularly when the first electrode is formed from a transparent conductive material having comparatively high sheet resistance, a metallic current-spreading structure is arranged on the first electrode. The current-spreading structure may, for example, take the form of conductive tracks, a grid, or another patterned metallization extending over at least part of the active area.

The metallic current-spreading structure is covered by an inorganic passivation layer containing one or more metal sulfides, metal selenides, and/or metal tellurides. Suitable materials may be selected to provide semiconducting behavior and sufficient chemical and thermal stability under the conditions used to fabricate and operate the component. The passivation layer can conformally cover the upper surface and sidewalls of the metallic structure, thereby separating it from the subsequently deposited organic functional layer stack.

Although the passivation material is semiconducting, its electrical properties and the energy-level alignment at the relevant interfaces suppress or substantially prevent direct current flow between the current-spreading structure and the organic functional layers. Consequently, charge carriers are introduced into the organic stack primarily through the first electrode rather than directly through the metal tracks. This reduces the risk of local current injection, leakage paths, short circuits, excessive heating, and nonuniform light emission in regions adjacent to the current-spreading structure.

At the same time, the metal structure remains electrically coupled to the first electrode and lowers its effective lateral resistance. Current can therefore be distributed more uniformly over a large light-emitting area without the metal structure electrically interfering with the organic functional stack. The resulting component may exhibit improved emission uniformity, reduced voltage loss, enhanced operational reliability, and greater suitability for large-area organic light-emitting diodes and related optoelectronic devices.

### The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the smallest yet most frequently used words in the English language. Known as the definite article, it identifies a particular person, place, object, or idea. For example, “the book” refers to a specific book, while “a book” could mean any book.

Despite its simplicity, “the” plays an essential role in clear communication. It helps listeners and readers understand whether something is already known, unique, or especially important. We say “the sun” because there is only one sun in our everyday context, and “the answer” when a particular answer is expected.

The word may be easy to overlook, but English would be far less precise without it.

counterfactuals.prompt: How can a metal current spreading structure be incorporated into an organic light-emitting device without allowing current to flow directly between the structure and the organic functional layer stack?
counterfactuals.output:
Incorporate the metal current-spreading structure as a bus grid connected to the device electrode, but cover all metal surfaces facing the organic stack with a dielectric isolation layer.

A typical sequence is:

1. Form the transparent electrode on the substrate.
2. Pattern a conductive metal grid or bus lines in electrical contact with that electrode.
3. Deposit and pattern an insulating/passivation layer over the top and sidewalls of the metal, preferably also planarizing the grid edges.
4. Deposit the organic functional layers and counter-electrode over the insulated structure.

The metal then carries current laterally and feeds it into the transparent electrode, while the dielectric cap prevents direct metal-to-organic current injection, shorts, field concentration, and damage to the organic layers. Electrical contact is retained only at selected interfaces or vias between the metal grid and the intended electrode.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical description of an OLED architecture featuring an n-type or p-type inorganic passivation layer formed from a metal chalcogenide over a conductive current spreading structure.
counterfactuals.output:
An organic light-emitting diode (OLED) architecture includes a substrate supporting a first electrode, an organic electroluminescent stack, and a second electrode. The organic stack may include one or more charge-injection, charge-transport, emissive, and charge-blocking layers disposed between the first and second electrodes. At least one electrode, preferably a transparent or semitransparent electrode, is electrically coupled to a conductive current-spreading structure such as a metal grid, nanowire network, conductive oxide pattern, graphene layer, or interconnected metal mesh. The current-spreading structure lowers lateral sheet resistance and promotes uniform current injection across the OLED emission area.

An inorganic passivation layer is formed over and conformally covers at least the conductive current-spreading structure. The passivation layer comprises an n-type or p-type metal chalcogenide, including a metal sulfide, selenide, or telluride. Suitable n-type materials include ZnS, ZnSe, CdS, CdSe, SnS₂, In₂S₃, MoS₂, or WS₂, while suitable p-type materials include NiS, Cu₂S, CuS, SnS, MoTe₂, or WSe₂, with conductivity type selected through composition, stoichiometry, substitutional doping, or defect control. The layer may have a thickness of approximately 1–200 nm and can be deposited by atomic-layer deposition, chemical-vapor deposition, sputtering, evaporation, solution processing, or chalcogenization of a predeposited metal layer.

The metal-chalcogenide layer electrically and chemically passivates the current-spreading structure, suppressing oxidation, corrosion, ion migration, and metal diffusion into adjacent organic or electrode layers. Its conductivity type and energy levels may be selected to provide favorable carrier transfer between the current-spreading structure and the associated OLED electrode. An n-type passivation layer can facilitate electron injection or extraction near a cathodic contact, whereas a p-type layer can facilitate hole injection or extraction near an anodic contact. The passivation layer may remain sufficiently resistive in the through-plane or lateral direction to prevent short circuits while retaining adequate carrier transport at contact regions.

An optional transparent dielectric barrier or encapsulation layer may be disposed over the metal-chalcogenide passivation layer to further inhibit oxygen and moisture ingress. Contact openings can be formed through the passivation and barrier layers for connection to external drive circuitry. This arrangement provides reduced electrode voltage drop, improved emission uniformity, enhanced environmental stability, and reduced degradation caused by direct interaction between the conductive current-spreading material and the OLED stack.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
